case_analysis.focal_point: Whether federal courts have jurisdiction to review the Department of Homeland Security’s revocation of an approved immigrant visa petition under 8 U.S.C. § 1155, or whether such revocations are barred from judicial review by the INA’s jurisdiction-stripping provision in 8 U.S.C. § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii).
case_analysis.legal_provision: 8 U.S.C. § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) (bar on judicial review of discretionary immigration decisions specified by statute) and 8 U.S.C. § 1155 (authority to revoke approval of visa petitions “for what he deems to be good and sufficient cause”).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The petitioner argues that § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) does not eliminate judicial review of visa-petition revocations under § 1155 because Congress did not clearly and unambiguously bar review of these revocations; at minimum, courts should be able to review whether the agency complied with statutory limits and basic legal requirements (e.g., acted within the scope of delegated authority, applied the correct legal standard, and provided a legally sufficient basis), rather than treating revocation decisions as entirely unreviewable.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The respondents argue that § 1155 expressly commits revocations to the Secretary’s discretion (including the phrases “may,” “at any time,” and “for what he deems to be good and sufficient cause”), and because that discretion is “specified” in Title II of the INA, § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) strips district courts of jurisdiction to review revocation decisions; the Eleventh Circuit’s approach is consistent with the statute’s text and Congress’s decision to preclude judicial review of discretionary immigration judgments.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s presumption-of-reviewability point (St. Cyr; Abbott Labs) is the hardest issue, and I share Justice Jackson’s concern about insulating unlawful action. But Kucana’s clear-statement principle is satisfied here because § 1155 itself specifies discretion in unusually direct terms—“may,” “at any time,” and “for what he deems to be good and sufficient cause”—bringing the revocation decision within § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) as Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch emphasize. Patel reinforces that we cannot preserve jurisdiction by re-labeling a challenge to the Secretary’s discretionary cause determination as a “legal” claim when adjudicating it would require second-guessing what the Secretary “deems” sufficient cause. The narrow, legitimacy-preserving course is to hold only that courts lack jurisdiction to review the discretionary revocation judgment itself, while leaving open genuinely independent constitutional or pure legal claims not presented here.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s presumption-of-reviewability point (St. Cyr; Abbott Labs) is the best counter, but under a textualist approach it cannot overcome Congress’s clear jurisdictional withdrawal in § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) for “any other decision or action” whose authority is “specified” by statute to be discretionary. Section 1155 does exactly what Kucana requires—specifies discretion by statute—by authorizing revocation “at any time, for what [the Secretary] deems to be good and sufficient cause,” so Kucana cuts in Respondent’s favor, as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan explain. Justice Jackson’s attempt to preserve “antecedent legal questions” fails where adjudicating the purported “legal” claim would still require a court to second-guess what the Secretary “deems” sufficient—precisely the kind of merits review Patel cautions courts not to repackage. Any residual space for genuinely collateral constitutional claims does not justify creating APA-style legality review of the revocation determination itself when the text does not preserve it.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s strongest point is the St. Cyr/Abbott Labs presumption of reviewability for legal-limit claims, but that presumption yields where Congress has spoken with unusual clarity. Here, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch stress, § 1155’s “may, at any time, for what he deems to be good and sufficient cause” is a statutory specification of discretion that satisfies Kucana’s clear-statement requirement and thus triggers § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii)’s jurisdictional bar. Patel reinforces that courts cannot evade that bar by relabeling a merits attack on the revocation (and its asserted “legal” predicates) as a pure legal challenge when adjudication would necessarily second-guess what the Secretary “deems” sufficient cause. I agree with Roberts that we should be careful not to opine more broadly than necessary: genuinely independent constitutional claims may remain, but ordinary APA-style review of the revocation decision itself is foreclosed by the text.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I accept Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Gorsuch’s strongest textual point that § 1155 specifies broad discretion over the ultimate revocation decision (“may…for what he deems…good and sufficient cause”), satisfying Kucana’s statute-based requirement and triggering § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) as to merits second-guessing. But Justice Thomas and Justice Alito press Patel too far: Patel bars review that would require reweighing discretionary judgments or their factual predicates, yet it does not clearly eliminate jurisdiction to decide whether the agency stayed within statutory bounds or applied the correct legal framework—questions that can be resolved without substituting a court’s view of “cause” for the Secretary’s. Under St. Cyr and Abbott Labs’ presumption of reviewability and the clear-statement rule, I cannot read “for what he deems” as an unmistakable instruction to insulate ultra vires or legally erroneous action from any judicial check, especially where the real-world consequences for families are severe. So I would hold revocation merits are unreviewable, but courts retain jurisdiction over genuinely legal and constitutional limits claims (as Justice Jackson urges), and this case should proceed at least to that extent.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s St. Cyr/Abbott Labs presumption-of-review point is serious, but it cannot displace the unusually explicit statutory commitment to discretion in § 1155—“may,” “at any time,” and “for what he deems to be good and sufficient cause”—which, under Kucana, is the kind of statute-based specification that triggers § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii). Justice Jackson’s effort to carve out “antecedent legal questions” is appealing in the abstract, but in this setting most alleged legal errors collapse into a challenge to whether the Secretary had (or adequately articulated) “good and sufficient cause,” inviting the very APA-style second-guessing Patel warns courts not to permit through relabeling. I find Chief Justice Roberts’s narrowing move persuasive: hold only that jurisdiction is barred as to review of the revocation judgment itself, without opining broadly about truly independent constitutional or purely legal claims that do not seek merits review. On a pragmatic textualist reading, that approach best preserves statutory coherence—giving effect to Congress’s jurisdictional bar while avoiding unnecessary dicta that would foreclose genuinely collateral claims in future cases.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the presumption of reviewability and insist § 1155 specifies discretion only as to the ultimate revocation, not antecedent legal limits. But under a textualist approach, § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) bars review of “any … decision or action” whose authority is “specified under this subchapter to be in the discretion” of the Secretary, and § 1155’s “may, at any time, for what he deems to be good and sufficient cause” is an unusually explicit statutory commitment of that decision to discretion, satisfying Kucana’s statute-based clear-statement requirement. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan note, allowing APA-style “legal error” review here would largely collapse into reassessing whether the Secretary had “good and sufficient cause” as he “deems,” which Patel cautions courts not to repackage as reviewable. I remain open to genuinely freestanding constitutional or purely legal claims that do not seek to overturn the discretionary revocation judgment itself, but that narrower possibility does not supply jurisdiction for the claim presented.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson rightly press the St. Cyr/Abbott Labs presumption that Congress must speak clearly before foreclosing a forum for legal error, and I take that concern seriously as an institutional matter. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, Kucana’s clear-statement principle is satisfied here because § 1155 itself specifies sweeping discretion—“may, at any time, for what he deems to be good and sufficient cause”—which triggers § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii)’s jurisdictional bar by its terms. Patel further supports rejecting efforts to relabel a merits challenge to the Secretary’s “good and sufficient cause” judgment as a “legal” claim, because adjudicating such a claim would necessarily second-guess what the Secretary “deems” sufficient. I would therefore hold the revocation determination unreviewable while leaving open, as Roberts suggests, only genuinely independent constitutional or purely collateral legal claims not seeking APA-style review of the revocation’s merits.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the strongest objection: that even if § 1155 commits the ultimate revocation judgment to discretion, the presumption of reviewability (St. Cyr; Abbott Labs) should preserve jurisdiction over “pure” legal-limit claims. But under a textualist reading, § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) withdraws jurisdiction over “any … decision or action” whose authority is “specified” by statute to be discretionary, and § 1155 does precisely that by making revocation turn on what the Secretary “deems” good and sufficient cause “at any time,” satisfying Kucana’s clear-statement requirement as Chief Justice Roberts explains. Patel further confirms that courts cannot evade such a jurisdictional bar by relabeling disagreements with a discretionary determination (and its predicates) as legal error when adjudication would necessarily second-guess what the Secretary “deems” sufficient. I agree with the Chief Justice’s narrowing caution: any residual review must be limited to genuinely independent constitutional or purely legal questions that do not seek review of the revocation decision’s merits, and nothing presented here fits that description.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan make the best textual case that § 1155’s “may…at any time…for what he deems” is an unusually direct statutory specification of discretion that triggers § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii), especially under Kucana’s statute-based focus and Patel’s warning against relabeling merits disputes as “legal” claims. But that argument still does not supply the clear statement needed to foreclose review of genuinely antecedent legal limits—i.e., whether the agency acted within the statutory framework and followed required procedures—because Congress specified discretion over the ultimate revocation judgment, not an unreviewable license to act ultra vires. Under St. Cyr and Abbott Laboratories’ presumption of reviewability, I would read the jurisdictional bar to block courts from reweighing whether “good and sufficient cause” exists, while preserving a narrow channel for pure legal/process challenges that can be resolved without second-guessing what the Secretary “deems” sufficient. Patel’s breadth is real, but it does not compel collapsing every legal-boundary question into an unreviewable “predicate” when the court can decide the issue without revisiting the discretionary weighing Congress committed to the agency.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) bars judicial review of any “decision or action” whose “authority” is “specified under this subchapter to be in the discretion” of the Secretary, and § 1155 squarely grants discretionary authority to revoke an approved petition—“may, at any time, for what he deems to be good and sufficient cause.” Reading those provisions together, the revocation determination is the kind of discretionary judgment Congress insulated from review, consistent with Patel v. Garland’s instruction that § 1252(a)(2)(B) reaches discretionary determinations and their predicates. Kucana v. Holder counsels that jurisdiction-stripping must be tied to discretion “specified” by statute, but here the statute itself uses classic discretionary terms, making this a narrow, text-based holding that preserves institutional legitimacy by adhering to Congress’s chosen limits. Any residual review would be confined, at most, to genuinely legal or constitutional questions not presented by a challenge to the Secretary’s “good and sufficient cause” judgment.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) strips jurisdiction over “any other decision or action” for which authority is “specified under” Title II to be in the Secretary’s “discretion,” and § 1155—located in Title II—specifies precisely that: the Secretary “may, at any time, for what he deems to be good and sufficient cause, revoke” an approved petition. Under Patel v. Garland, “any” is expansive and the jurisdictional bar reaches discretionary determinations Congress has specified by statute, not merely those committed to discretion by regulation. Section 1155’s “for what he deems” language makes the revocation judgment itself discretionary, so courts lack jurisdiction to repackage review as scrutiny of the agency’s asserted reasons. Absent a separate statutory preservation of review (cf. § 1252(a)(2)(D) for certain petitions for review), the plain text controls and forecloses district-court review here.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) strips jurisdiction over decisions that a statute "specif[ies]" to be in the Secretary’s discretion, and § 1155 does exactly that by providing the Secretary "may, at any time" revoke approval "for what he deems to be good and sufficient cause." Under Patel v. Garland, Congress’s jurisdiction-stripping in § 1252(a)(2)(B) is to be enforced according to its text, and courts may not repackage disagreement with the agency’s judgment as reviewable legal error when the statute commits the determination to discretionary assessment. Kucana v. Holder reinforces that the bar turns on discretion specified by statute (as here), not discretion supplied only by regulation. While St. Cyr recognized review of pure questions of law in other contexts, § 1155’s "deems" formulation makes the core revocation determination an exercise of discretion that Congress chose to insulate from judicial second-guessing.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) strips jurisdiction only where Congress clearly specifies that a particular decision is discretionary, and we apply a strong presumption favoring judicial review—especially of legal questions—absent an unambiguous statement to the contrary. Kucana v. Holder instructs that this jurisdiction-stripping provision must be read narrowly and with a clear-statement rule, and nothing in § 1155’s “for what he deems to be good and sufficient cause” language clearly eliminates review of whether DHS acted within statutory limits or applied the correct legal standard. Reading § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) to foreclose any forum for correcting legal or constitutional error in visa-petition revocations would be a drastic result inconsistent with St. Cyr and Abbott Laboratories’ presumption of reviewability and would risk severe, real-world harms to families and other vulnerable petitioners. Courts should at least retain jurisdiction to review legal and constitutional challenges to § 1155 revocations, even if they cannot second-guess discretionary weighing of facts.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) withdraws jurisdiction over any decision whose authority is “specified under this subchapter to be in the discretion” of the Secretary, and § 1155 does exactly that by authorizing revocation “for what he deems to be good and sufficient cause,” “at any time,” and by use of “may,” all of which signal a judgment committed to the Secretary’s discretion. Kucana v. Holder requires that the discretion be specified by statute (not regulation), and § 1155’s text meets that clarity threshold, unlike the regulation-based discretion rejected in Kucana. Patel v. Garland reinforces that when Congress uses sweeping jurisdiction-stripping language tied to discretionary immigration judgments, courts may not repackage merits challenges as legal ones; any remaining review would be limited to truly collateral constitutional claims, not whether “good and sufficient cause” existed. Reading the scheme pragmatically, allowing APA-style review of the sufficiency of the Secretary’s cause determination would largely defeat Congress’s choice to insulate specified discretionary immigration decisions from judicial second-guessing.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) withdraws jurisdiction over any decision whose authority is “specified under this subchapter to be in the discretion” of the Secretary, and § 1155 (in the same subchapter) provides that the Secretary “may, at any time, for what he deems to be good and sufficient cause” revoke an approved petition—text that squarely commits the revocation judgment to executive discretion. Under Kucana v. Holder, the jurisdictional bar applies when discretion is specified by statute (not merely regulation), and § 1155 does exactly that through its “may” and “deems” formulations. Patel v. Garland reinforces that when Congress uses broad language to preclude review of discretionary immigration decisions, courts may not recharacterize challenges as review of “legal” questions if they would require second-guessing the discretionary determination Congress committed to the agency. Whatever the background presumption favoring review (Abbott Laboratories; St. Cyr), the plain text here supplies the requisite clear statement, leaving only any constitutional claims outside the bar, not ordinary APA review of the revocation decision itself.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) strips jurisdiction over “any other decision or action” where the authority is “specified under this subchapter to be in the discretion” of the Secretary, and § 1155’s text (“may,” “at any time,” and “for what he deems to be good and sufficient cause”) specifies broad discretionary revocation authority. Under Patel v. Garland, this Court has read § 1252(a)(2)(B) broadly to foreclose judicial review of discretionary immigration determinations even when litigants repackage challenges as legal or factual disputes connected to those decisions. Kucana v. Holder’s “specified by statute” requirement is satisfied here because the discretion is conferred by § 1155 itself (not merely by regulation), and the Court should be reluctant to create a carve-out that would invite routine litigation and undermine the INA’s channeling of immigration disputes. Absent an express statutory preservation of review for § 1155 revocations akin to other INA provisions, the most workable and precedent-consistent reading is that these revocations fall within § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii)’s jurisdictional bar.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) strips jurisdiction over any “decision or action” whose authority is “specified under this subchapter to be in the discretion” of the Secretary, and § 1155—located in that subchapter—authorizes the Secretary to revoke approvals when he “may, at any time, for what he deems to be good and sufficient cause” to do so. Under Kucana v. Holder, the presumption of review yields where Congress has clearly specified discretion by statute; § 1155’s “may,” “at any time,” and “for what he deems” language is precisely the kind of statutory specification that triggers § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii). Patel v. Garland reinforces that when Congress withdraws jurisdiction over discretionary determinations, courts may not repackage challenges as legal ones to obtain review of the discretionary judgment itself. Given this statutory scheme and the breadth of discretion conferred, federal courts lack jurisdiction to review § 1155 revocations except to the extent a claim independently fits within a preserved constitutional or pure legal question not seeking review of the discretionary revocation decision.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) strips jurisdiction only when a statute “specif[ies]” that the relevant decision is committed to agency discretion, and the Court has required a clear statement before reading the INA to foreclose judicial review of legal constraints on agency action. Although § 1155 uses discretionary language (“may,” “at any time,” and “for what he deems to be good and sufficient cause”), it does not clearly and unambiguously preclude courts from reviewing threshold legal questions—such as whether DHS applied the correct standard, acted within statutory bounds, or provided a legally sufficient rationale—consistent with the strong presumption in favor of judicial review recognized in INS v. St. Cyr and Abbott Laboratories. Reading § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) to bar all review would risk insulating potentially unlawful action from any Article III check, a result the Court has been reluctant to attribute to Congress absent unmistakable clarity. This limited legality review also harmonizes Kucana’s insistence that jurisdiction-stripping be grounded in statutory text with Patel’s recognition that Congress can preclude review of discretionary judgments, without extending that bar to pure questions of law.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether federal courts have jurisdiction to review the Secretary of Homeland Security’s decision to revoke approval of an immigrant visa petition under 8 U.S.C. § 1155, or whether that decision is barred from judicial review by 8 U.S.C. § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii).
case_analysis.legal_provision: 8 U.S.C. § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) (jurisdiction-stripping for discretionary immigration decisions specified by statute) and 8 U.S.C. § 1155 (authority to revoke approved visa petitions “for what he deems to be good and sufficient cause”).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that § 1155 revocations should remain judicially reviewable (at least for legal and procedural errors) because the jurisdiction-stripping clause in § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) should be read narrowly, and § 1155’s “good and sufficient cause” language supplies a legal standard that courts can apply; eliminating review would allow arbitrary or legally erroneous revocations to escape any meaningful check, undermining the rule of law and disrupting reliance interests of families, employers, and investors whose immigration eligibility depends on approved petitions.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) strips courts of jurisdiction because § 1155 expressly commits revocation decisions to the Secretary’s discretion (“may,” “at any time,” and “for what he deems to be good and sufficient cause”), making revocation a quintessential discretionary act specified by Title II of the INA; therefore, district courts cannot review revocations, and Congress intended to preclude such review to preserve agency flexibility over admissions-related determinations.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson forcefully invoke Kucana’s presumption of reviewability and argue that “good and sufficient cause” supplies a manageable limit, but § 1155’s operative phrasing—revocation “for what he deems to be good and sufficient cause”—shifts the standard from an objective legal yardstick to the Secretary’s own evaluative judgment, leaving courts no principled metric to apply without substituting their view. Justice Kavanaugh’s Chaney/Webster analogy is not merely an APA backdrop; it reinforces the core textual point that when Congress keys the trigger to what the official “deems,” it signals the kind of discretion that § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) captures, especially after Patel’s broad reading of “any decision or action.” The contrast Justice Jackson draws to § 1201(i) is relevant but not dispositive: Congress can foreclose review either via an explicit no-review clause or by specifying discretionary authority that activates clause (ii), and here the statutory language is sufficiently clear to do the latter. The narrow, legitimacy-preserving course is to hold the discretionary merits of § 1155 revocations unreviewable under § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii), while leaving open any review Congress elsewhere preserves for colorable constitutional claims or pure questions of law in a proper procedural posture.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson’s strongest point is that “good and sufficient cause” can operate as a limiting standard preserving at least legal/procedural review, aided by Kucana’s presumption of reviewability and the contrast to § 1201(i). But the text of § 1155 does not impose an objective “cause” test; it authorizes revocation for what the Secretary “deems” to be good and sufficient cause, and that subjective delegation—paired with “may” and “at any time”—is precisely the sort of discretion “specified under this subchapter” that triggers § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) under Kucana. As Justice Kavanaugh notes with Chaney/Webster, when Congress frames the operative criterion in terms of the official’s own deeming, courts lack a manageable legal yardstick without substituting their judgment for the Secretary’s, which a textualist/originalist approach cannot do to preserve review. I therefore remain with the Chief Justice and the other respondents: whatever residual review might exist for colorable constitutional claims or pure questions of law via an independent statutory hook, the merits of § 1155 revocations fall within the jurisdictional bar Congress wrote.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the strongest point: that “good and sufficient cause” supplies a judicially administrable standard and that we should apply Kucana’s presumption of reviewability. But § 1155 does not ask whether there is “good and sufficient cause” in some objective sense; it authorizes revocation for what the Secretary “deems” to be good and sufficient cause, coupled with “may” and “at any time,” which is precisely the kind of subjective delegation that leaves no meaningful standard for courts to apply and thus falls within § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii). Justice Kavanaugh’s analogy to Webster v. Doe and Heckler v. Chaney reinforces that when Congress commits the triggering judgment to the official’s own view, review of the merits is foreclosed even if the agency must use certain words. The comparison Justice Jackson draws to § 1201(i)’s express bar does not overcome the text here; Congress can preclude review either by an explicit no-review clause or by specifying discretionary authority that triggers § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii), and § 1155’s language is clear enough to do the latter.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s textual point—that “for what he deems” makes the judgment discretionary and thus triggers § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii)—is the strongest case for the Respondent, especially after Patel’s broad reading of “any decision or action.” But even accepting that § 1155 commits the ultimate weighing to the Secretary, it does not follow that Congress clearly foreclosed judicial power to police legal error and basic procedural regularity where the statute still contains a constraint (“good and sufficient cause”) and where Kucana instructs us to construe jurisdiction-stripping narrowly absent an unmistakable statement. Justice Kavanaugh’s invocation of Chaney and Webster helps identify why courts should not second-guess the merits, yet those cases address APA reviewability and do not compel reading clause (ii) to extinguish all judicial forums for claims that the agency acted outside statutory bounds, ignored mandatory procedures, or relied on impermissible reasons. Given the severe reliance interests and risk of unchecked arbitrariness, I would preserve at least limited review for legal/procedural defects rather than treat “deems” as a wholesale ouster of jurisdiction.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson are right to insist on a presumption of reviewability and to note that “good and sufficient cause” sounds like a constraint, but § 1155’s operative grant is revocation for what the Secretary “deems” to be good and sufficient cause—text that makes the criterion the Secretary’s judgment rather than an objective, judicially enforceable standard. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize (drawing on Webster/Chaney), that kind of “deems” formulation is exactly how Congress specifies discretionary authority in a way that fits § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) under Kucana, and Patel’s breadth about “any … decision or action” further counsels against carving out merits or procedural review by implication. Justice Jackson’s comparison to § 1201(i) shows Congress can speak even more explicitly, but it does not negate that Congress also enacted a cross-cutting jurisdictional bar keyed to statutorily specified discretion, which is satisfied here. I would still understand the holding to leave untouched whatever review exists for colorable constitutional claims or pure questions of law where another jurisdictional provision affirmatively supplies a forum, but § 1155’s revocation determination itself falls within clause (ii).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson are right to emphasize Kucana’s presumption of reviewability and the intuition that “good and sufficient cause” sounds like a legal constraint. But § 1155 does not set an objective cause standard; it authorizes revocation for what the Secretary “deems” to be good and sufficient cause, and that subjective formulation is precisely what Justice Kavanaugh (invoking Chaney/Webster) identifies as leaving courts without a judicially manageable yardstick—thus satisfying Kucana’s requirement that Congress itself “specified” discretion for purposes of § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii). The comparison to § 1201(i)’s express no-review clause, which Justice Jackson stresses, shows Congress can draft in different ways, not that it must repeat an explicit bar when the general jurisdictional bar already applies by its terms to “any decision or action” specified as discretionary. Fairness concerns cannot justify narrowing an unqualified jurisdictional limitation; whatever residual review exists must come, as the Chief Justice notes, through Congress’s separate preservation of constitutional claims or pure questions of law, not by recharacterizing a discretionary revocation judgment as reviewable.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s strongest point is that we can preserve limited review for legal or procedural defects without reweighing the merits, and she stresses Congress’s use of explicit no-review clauses elsewhere (e.g., § 1201(i)). But under Kucana the jurisdictional trigger is whether the statute itself specifies discretion, and § 1155’s phrasing—“may,” “at any time,” and critically “for what he deems to be good and sufficient cause”—makes the operative cause determination subjective in the same way we have treated as effectively standardless in Chaney and Webster, bringing it within § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii)’s “any decision or action” as Patel reads it broadly. Justice Sotomayor’s presumption-of-reviewability argument cannot overcome that Congress used classic discretionary terms; courts can’t convert “deems” into an objective yardstick without rewriting the delegation. I agree with the Chief Justice that we should leave open review only where Congress has separately preserved a jurisdictional hook for colorable constitutional claims or pure questions of law, but the merits of a § 1155 revocation are barred.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson are right to emphasize Kucana’s presumption of reviewability and the intuition that “good and sufficient cause” can operate as a constraint. But § 1155 does not impose an objective “good and sufficient cause” test; it authorizes revocation for what the Secretary “deems” to be good and sufficient cause, and that subjective formulation—paired with “may” and “at any time”—is the statutory specification of discretion that triggers § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) under Kucana, as the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh explain. The § 1201(i) comparison is not a clear-statement trump card: Congress can preclude review either by an express no-review clause or by using discretionary terms that activate clause (ii), and Patel reinforces that “any decision or action” sweeps broadly once discretion is specified. To the extent petitioners seek review of legal/procedural defects, those concerns go to what residual avenues (e.g., colorable constitutional claims) may remain, not to rewriting § 1155’s “deems” into a judicially enforceable merits standard.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s textual point—that “for what he deems” in § 1155 is a classic marker of discretion and thus triggers § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) under Kucana and Patel—is the strongest case for Respondent, and I take it seriously. But even accepting that the Secretary has broad evaluative space, the presence of “good and sufficient cause” still supplies a limiting principle that can support at least review for legal error and basic procedural regularity without inviting courts to second-guess the Secretary’s weighing, and I am not convinced Congress clearly meant clause (ii) to extinguish that minimum safeguard. Webster/Chaney (as Justice Kavanaugh emphasizes) matters as an APA analog for why merits review may be narrow, yet those cases do not compel reading a jurisdiction-stripping provision to wipe out all judicial policing of statutory and procedural boundaries absent a clearer statement—especially where Congress has shown it can foreclose review expressly, as Justice Sotomayor notes by comparison to other INA provisions. Given the serious fairness consequences of leaving even plainly unlawful revocations without a forum, I would preserve limited review for legal/procedural defects while recognizing that discretionary merits judgments remain insulated.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) strips jurisdiction over any decision or action that the INA itself “specif[ies]” to be in the Secretary’s discretion, and § 1155 does exactly that by providing the Secretary “may, at any time, for what he deems to be good and sufficient cause” revoke an approved petition. Under Kucana v. Holder, the touchstone is whether Congress (not the agency) specified discretionary authority; here Congress used classic discretionary terms (“may,” “at any time,” “deems”), indicating revocation decisions fall within clause (ii). To preserve institutional legitimacy while respecting Congress’s allocation of authority in immigration, the narrow course is to hold courts lack jurisdiction to review the revocation’s discretionary merits, while leaving room for review of colorable constitutional claims or pure questions of law where another provision supplies jurisdiction. This reading avoids rewriting § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) and accords with federalism and separation-of-powers limits on judicial supervision of admissions-related judgments.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) withdraws jurisdiction over any “decision or action” whose authority is “specified under this subchapter to be in the discretion” of the Secretary, and § 1155—within that subchapter—provides that the Secretary “may, at any time, for what he deems to be good and sufficient cause, revoke” an approved petition. Those words (“may,” “at any time,” and “what he deems”) plainly commit the revocation determination to the Secretary’s discretion, thereby triggering the jurisdictional bar. Kucana v. Holder confirms that the jurisdiction-stripping inquiry turns on whether discretion is specified by statute (not merely regulation), and here it is specified by § 1155 itself. Whatever prudential concerns exist about arbitrariness, they cannot overcome Congress’s clear textual choice to preclude judicial review of this discretionary decision.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) withdraws jurisdiction over any decision “the authority for which is specified under this subchapter to be in the discretion” of the Secretary, and § 1155—within that subchapter—provides that the Secretary “may, at any time, for what he deems to be good and sufficient cause, revoke” an approved petition. The repeated discretionary signals (“may,” “at any time,” and especially “for what he deems”) indicate Congress specified this revocation authority as discretionary, leaving no meaningful judicially manageable standard for courts to apply. While Kucana v. Holder recognizes a presumption of reviewability, it also requires “clear and convincing evidence” to rebut it, and § 1155’s text supplies that evidence by committing both the timing and the cause determination to the Secretary’s judgment. Allowing judicial review here would invite courts to second-guess admissions-related discretionary judgments Congress chose to entrust to the Executive, undermining the practical need for flexibility in immigration administration.
